rationale_summary: The Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights is overwhelmingly framed around fundamental_rights: its stated purpose is to protect civil rights, civil liberties, personal-data privacy, non-discrimination, equity for underserved communities, human dignity, and democratic values against harms from automated systems. Fundamental_rights decisively leads consumer_public_safety, which serves as the main secondary frame via protections against unsafe clinical tools, stalking devices, non-consensual intimate imagery, and defective automated systems. Labor_transition (workplace surveillance chilling union organizing, automated firing without recourse, algorithmic quotas/bonuses) and innovation_enablement ('clear rules of the road that allow new ideas to flourish') appear as distinct supporting frames, alongside minor social_stability (trust and democratic process) and national_security (disclaimer carve-out) mentions.

evidence_spans.quote: Among the great challenges posed to democracy today is the use of technology, data, and automated systems in ways that threaten the rights of the American public.
It is intended to support the development of policies and practices that protect civil rights and promote democratic values in the building, deployment, and governance of automated systems.
In America and around the world, systems supposed to help with patient care have proven unsafe, ineffective, or biased.
Automated systems should not be designed with an intent or reasonably foreseeable possibility of endangering your safety or the safety of your community.

A large corporation automated performance evaluation and other HR functions, leading to workers being fired by an automated system without the possibility of human review, appeal or other form of recourse.104

evidence_spans.quote: Innovators deserve clear rules of the road that allow new ideas to flourish, and the American public deserves protections from unsafe outcomes.
